newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile denies it risking South American arms race.
newsitem.headline: Chile denies it risking South American arms race.

text.p: Chile denied on Monday it was triggering a South American arms race, despite reports it is shopping for F-16 fighter jets and maintaining one of the region's highest defence spending rates.
"We maintain spending levels that allow us to protect our borders like any other country and, in general, we are not in any arms race," said acting Foreign Minister Mariano Fernandez.
"On the contrary, I think Chile is carrying out a very prudent defence policy," he told a news conference.

Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter said in Brazil last week he hoped Chile would not go ahead with plans to buy sophisticated F-16s, or some other jet like them, because to do so risked starting a new regional arms race.
Carter said any such purchase would have especially serious consequences in neighbouring Argentina, which has cut its defence spending to the bone in the past five years.
The two countries, which share a long Andean border, have had a string of border disputes over the years although relations are currently considered good and only one dispute is still pending.

Fernandez, who did not refer specifically to the possible F-16 purchase, said studies showing Chile with a high defence budget included spending on military pensions and on salaries for civilian personnel, categories not included for other countries.

"So what you have is an overstating of the spending. As far as outlays strictly on defence are concerned, we've actually diminished them," said Fernandez. "We have a reduction in (defense) spending in relation to gross domestic product, and that's the important thing."

But a study released last year by the U.N. Development Programme showed Chilean defence spending at 3.5 percent of GDP -- the highest in all of Latin America, higher than Cuba or Ecuador, which has an active border dispute with Peru.
Argentina's defence spending rate was 1.7 percent of GDP, according to the report, which was cited last week in another report by the Inter American Development Bank.
Other studies have shown Chilean defence spending among the region's highest, although lower in real terms since the country emerged from 17 years of military rule in 1990.

Chilean defence officials have said they would be interested in modernising the air force with U.S. F-16s, if the Clinton administration lifts a 20-year-old virtual ban on sales of sophisticated U.S. materiel to Latin America.
Chile has already approached European makers of similar planes in case the U.S. ban is not lifted, officials have said.
